title: Blebitis: The Ticking Time Bomb of Glaucoma Surgery
summary: Blebitis is a sight-threatening localized infection of a filtration bleb, typically following trabeculectomy. Without rapid intervention, it frequently progresses to bleb-associated endophthalmitis (BAE), making it a critical emergency for the ophthalmologist.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Scope
sections.content: Blebitis is defined as a localized infection involving the filtering bleb, but notably lacking vitreous involvement. It is a precursor to Bleb-Associated Endophthalmitis (BAE). It occurs post-trabeculectomy or post-GDD, often months to years after the initial surgery (late-onset). The hallmark is a 'milky' appearance of the bleb contents due to purulent material (hypopyon within the bleb).

rows: Often more chronic or subacute presentation.
Highly virulent; rapid progression to Stage III.
Common in inferior blebs; very aggressive destruction.
Associated with poor hygiene or CL wear.
Milky bleb, erythema, NO AC reaction.
Cells/Flare or Hypopyon in AC; clear vitreous.

sections.title: Clinical Presentation: Red Flags
content: Sudden onset of ocular pain or 'deep ache'
Rapidly decreasing Visual Acuity
Purulent discharge from the bleb area
Photophobia and ciliary injection
Milky white or yellow 'pseudohypopyon' within the bleb

sections.title: Ocular Examination Findings
content: Slit Lamp: Opacified (milky) bleb with loss of translucency
Seidel Test: Critical to check for active bleb leaks
Conjunctival hyperemia (localized or diffuse)
AC: Tyndall effect (cells/flare), potentially hypopyon
Fundoscopy: Must rule out vitreous involvement (critical distinction)
B-Scan USG: Indicated if media opacity prevents fundus view

rows: Quiet eye, no pain, bleb is clear/white but not 'milky' or purulent.
No primary bleb focus; diffuse AC reaction.
Significant vitreous cells/haze; marked reduction in vision.
Hypotony, positive Seidel, but eye is usually quiet and not 'hot'.

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Protocol
content: Step 1: Immediate clinical assessment and slit-lamp photography.
Step 2: Conjunctival and bleb surface swabs for Culture (Blood agar, Chocolate, Thioglycollate).
Step 3: If AC reaction present, consider AC tap (though controversial in isolated blebitis).
Step 4: Dilated fundus exam with indirect ophthalmoscopy to assess vitreous.
Step 5: B-scan ultrasonography to rule out posterior segment involvement if view is obscured.

sections.title: Medical Management Strategy
content: Intensive Topical Therapy: Fluoroquinolones (Moxifloxacin) every 30-60 mins.
Fortified Antibiotics: Vancomycin (50mg/mL) + Tobramycin (14mg/mL) or Ceftazidime (50mg/mL).
Cycloplegics: Atropine 1% or Cyclopentolate 1% BID to prevent synechiae.
Oral Antibiotics: Moxifloxacin 400mg QD (good ocular penetration).
Topical Steroids: DELAY 24-48 hours until clinical improvement is noted.

sections.title: Surgical Intervention Indicators
content: Progression to Stage III (Endophthalmitis) requires Vitrectomy + Intravitreal antibiotics.
Persistent Bleb Leak: Requires surgical revision once infection clears.
Bleb Excision: Reserved for recurrent infection or intractable leaks.
Patch Grafting: Using sclera, cornea, or pericardium for structural reinforcement.

content.explanation: L: Lower lid position (Inferior bleb); E: Excessive Antimetabolites (MMC); A: Aqueous leak (Seidel +); K: Keratoconjunctivitis (Blepharitis); Y: Young age/High Myopia.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: A 'white' bleb is not always infected, but a 'milky' bleb always is.
Streptococcal blebitis can blind an eye within 24 hours—act aggressively.
Avoid inferior trabeculectomies whenever possible to reduce lifelong risk.
Lifelong education: Patients must report any 'red eye' immediately.
Ischemic, thin-walled blebs have a 5-10% lifetime risk of infection.

branches: Bleb Failure due to scarring post-infection

sections.title: Landmark Insights: CIGTS & Beyond
sections.content: The CIGTS (Collaborative Initial Glaucoma Treatment Study) and other long-term trabeculectomy cohorts highlighted that the risk of blebitis does not diminish over time; it is a cumulative lifetime risk. Modern surgical trends have shifted toward GDDs or MIGS in high-risk patients (like contact lens wearers or those with ocular surface disease) to avoid the vulnerable filtration bleb.
